# Building the office scene

Your mental model is right: make a room in Unity, put walls and desks in it, then the moving parts
get scripted. This is that, cut down to only what this game needs.

The part you are worried about is smaller than it looks, and most of it can be skipped. Read the
last section before you start dragging anything.

---

## Rule one, before anything else

**Do not build the office inside a scene.** Both scenes here are generated by
`ScalingLawsSceneBuilder`, and anything placed by hand is deleted the next time it runs.

**Build it as a prefab.** A prefab is a file on disk, not part of a scene, so the builder never
touches it. The builder drops it into the scene with one line. You author it visually, it survives
every rebuild.

Practically: everything below happens inside a prefab called `OfficeView`, not in `Game.unity`.

---

## Why 3D and not flat images

Post-processing, light that moves, and staff who walk need real geometry. A painted room has its
shadows baked in forever and a walking sprite needs a separate animation per direction.

It still reads as 2.5D, because the camera is orthographic and locked. Same look as the reference,
less work, and free CC0 kits are consistent by construction where a generated sprite set drifts.

---

## Assets

All CC0 unless noted. CC0 means no attribution and nothing to track at release.

**Start here**
- **Kenney Prototype Textures** (kenney.nl) - flat grey materials. Use these before any real art.
- **Kenney Furniture Kit** - desks, chairs, shelving, sofas, plants. The backbone.
- **Quaternius Ultimate Modular Interior** (quaternius.com) - walls, floors, doors, windows that
  snap together.
- **Quaternius Ultimate Modular Characters** - low poly people, **already rigged, with walk and idle
  animations included**. This single pack removes the entire rigging problem.

**If you want the exact look of the reference games**

The chunky low poly style in Devices Tycoon and Smartphone Tycoon is characteristic of **Synty
POLYGON** packs. I cannot confirm those studios use them, so treat that as a guess about the look
rather than a fact about their pipeline. Synty publishes a **free POLYGON Starter Pack** on their
site and on the Asset Store, which is enough to prototype an office in that style and decide whether
to buy `POLYGON Office` later.

Pick **one** interior kit and **one** furniture kit and stop. A kit plus a few extra pieces looks
like one set. Four kits looks like a collage, and no lighting fixes that.

---

## Setup, once

### URP

The package is already in the manifest, just not switched on.

1. **Assets > Create > Rendering > URP Asset (with Universal Renderer)**, save both files into
   `Assets/Settings/`.
2. **Project Settings > Graphics**, drag the URP Asset into **Scriptable Render Pipeline Settings**.
3. **Project Settings > Quality**, same for each level.
4. Magenta materials mean built-in shaders: select them, **Edit > Rendering > Materials > Convert
   Selected Built-in Materials to URP**.

### Camera

On the camera in `Game.unity`:

- Projection **Orthographic**, Size **6**
- Rotation **X 30, Y 45, Z 0**
- Position around `(10, 9, -10)`
- Tick **Post Processing** under Rendering, or nothing from the Volume renders

**Once the rotation is set, never change it.** Every placement decision assumes it.

### Light and post-processing

1. Directional Light: rotation around `X 50, Y -30`, Shadow Type **Soft Shadows**.
2. **Window > Rendering > Lighting**, Environment Lighting Source **Gradient**, cool sky and warm
   ground. This is what stops shadowed sides going flat black, and it is most of what people mean
   when they say a scene looks good.
3. **GameObject > Volume > Global Volume**, press **New** next to Profile, then **Add Override**:
   - **Tonemapping**, mode ACES. First, because everything else is judged through it.
   - **Vignette**, Intensity 0.25. Darkens the edges, which is exactly what the interface needs to
     stay readable over the scene.
   - **Bloom**, Threshold 1.1, Intensity 0.4. Monitors and status lights glow. Keep it low.
   - **Colour Adjustments**, Post Exposure +0.2, Saturation -8.
4. **Ambient occlusion is not a Volume override.** Select the Universal Renderer asset from step 1
   and **Add Renderer Feature > Screen Space Ambient Occlusion**. Biggest single improvement to an
   interior, nearly free.

---

## Building the room

1. **Create Empty**, name `OfficeView`, position `0,0,0`.
2. Empty children: `Room`, `Furniture`, `Staff`, `Servers`, `Waypoints`.
3. Under `Room`, build floor and walls from the modular kit. Hold **Ctrl** while dragging to snap;
   set the step in **Edit > Grid and Snap Settings** to match the kit, usually 1 or 2.
4. Under `Waypoints`, drop four to eight empty objects around the floor where people should walk.
   Position only; nothing else.
5. Leave `Furniture`, `Staff` and `Servers` **empty**. The game fills them at runtime.
6. Drag `OfficeView` into `Assets/_ScalingLaws/Prefabs/`. It turns blue. Delete the copy left in the
   Hierarchy.

That is the whole manual job: a floor, some walls, and a handful of empty markers.

### Import settings

Models: **Read/Write** off, **Import Cameras** off, **Import Lights** off. A downloaded kit will
otherwise drop a second camera into your scene and you will spend an hour wondering why the view is
wrong.

2D art: Texture Type **Sprite (2D and UI)**, Compression **High Quality**, **Generate Mip Maps off**.

---

## What gets scripted, and what that means for you

Desks, people and server racks are **not placed by hand**. The game already knows who is employed
and what hardware is owned, so it reads that and fills the room. Hire someone and a person appears
at a desk. Buy accelerators and racks appear. Let someone go and the desk empties.

I write that. What I need from you is the prefab with the floor, the walls and the waypoints, plus
the names of the kit prefabs you chose for desk, chair, person and rack.

---

## The shortcut, if the manual part still worries you

**I can generate the room layout in code as well.**

The scene builder already writes both scenes from an editor method. The same approach works for the
office: an editor script that places floor tiles, walls, desks and waypoints on a grid and saves the
result as a prefab. You would import a kit, tell me the prefab names, and run one menu command.

The trade is honest: code placement is fast, consistent and repeatable, but it will look like a grid,
because it is one. Hand placement is where a room stops looking generated. A good middle path is to
let the script lay out the floor, the walls and the desk grid, then move a few things by hand
afterwards, since editing a generated prefab is allowed and safe.

Say the word and I will write it. It is about an hour of work and it removes the part you are
dreading.

## Is there an AI that builds Unity scenes

Not really, and be careful with what claims otherwise. There are tools that generate 3D models from
text, and their output is usually unusable for a consistent art style. There is nothing that
composes a game scene to a brief at a quality worth keeping.

What genuinely helps is the thing above: describing the room once and having code place it. That is
the version of "AI builds the scene" that actually works, because the hard part was never the
placement, it was deciding what goes where.

---

## The order I would do it in

1. URP on, camera angle, light, volume. **No art at all.**
2. Grey-box: plain cubes with Kenney prototype materials. Ugly on purpose.
3. Tell me it exists. I write the spawner so staff and servers populate it from the save.
4. Swap grey boxes for the real kits, one piece at a time.

This matches the milestone in `CLAUDE.md`: a deliberately ugly grey-box build, so the economy can be
judged from the player's seat instead of from a test report. A grey box that runs beats a beautiful
room that does not.
